newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Replica of first Soviet Sputnik to go into orbit.
newsitem.headline: Replica of first Soviet Sputnik to go into orbit.

text.p: Russian cosmonauts will this autumn send into orbit a replica made by French children of the first Soviet Sputnik to mark the 40th anniversary of a launch that opened the modern era of space exploration.

A senior Mission Control official, speaking to reporters on Thursday as two cosmonauts returned safely after six months aboard the troubled Mir space station, said the replica would circle the earth for a year.
"The replica will transmit beeping signals from time to time, just like the original Sputnik One," said Viktor Blagov, deputy flight director at Mission Control just outside Moscow.
The replica, about a third the size of the original Sputnik, will be delivered to Mir in October by a supply ship and will be put into orbit manually by cosmonauts during a spacewalk, he said.

Soviet scientists launched Sputnik One, a small spherical satellite weighing about 50 kg, from the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan on October 4, 1957. It tracked the satellite's movements round the earth by its distinct beeping signals.
"The conquering of space has begun," said its designer Sergei Korolyov, the father of the Soviet space programme who gave his name to the town where Mission Control is situated.

On Thursday the Soyuz capsule carrying Commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin landed in the remote Kazakh steppes after a tough mission that raised questions about the future of Moscow's space programme.

The two cosmonauts, along with their NASA colleague Michael Foale who remains on Mir until next month, had endured a series of major problems, including a collision between the ageing space station and a supply ship on June 25.
